title: RNA G-quadruplexes in neurodegenerative disease: from structural regulation to proteinopathy.
abstract: RNA G-quadruplexes (rG4) are dynamic RNA structures whose cellular abundance and folded state are regulated by a multitude of factors. rG4-binding proteins (rG4BPs) comprise a diverse group, including intrinsically disordered proteins such as FUS, TDP-43, and α-Synuclein, which are associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Moreover, rG4 are elevated in human tissue or disease models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Parkinson's disease (PD), and Alzheimer's disease (AD), highlighting the importance of understanding the interplay between rG4 and rG4BPs. In this review, we examine the cellular mechanisms that regulate rG4 folding dynamics, with a particular focus on rG4BPs and cellular state. We outline the rG4BPs involved in ALS and PD, emphasizing their mechanisms of rG4 recognition. We discuss the current literature on the contributions of rG4s and rG4BPs to ALS, PD, AD, and Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) and their context-dependent effects on disease-associated protein phase transitions and aggregation. Finally, we highlight two emerging classes of molecules with therapeutic potential in neurodegenerative disease: rG4-containing and rG4-targeting. Together, this review explores the complex and context-dependent roles of rG4s in neurodegeneration and their potential as targets for manipulating RNA and protein biology.

title: AptaRender: an interactive drawing and styling tool for 2D nucleic acid structures.
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) diagrams are widely used to communicate nucleic acid secondary structure, yet the path from a sequence and pairing model to an editable publication figure often requires either specialized software or substantial cleanup in a general-purpose graphics editor. AptaRender (v2.3.1, available at https://yjhe99.github.io/aptarender/ ) is a browser-based editor that converts a set of user-supplied DNA or RNA sequences and their dot-bracket structures into an interactive 2D drawing. The software separates structure specification from visual composition: it does not predict folding, but provides direct control over the layout, nucleotide styling, base pair styling, numbering and export. AptaRender supports simultaneously working with multiple sequences, customized per-nucleotide sizing and coloring with customized styles, manual branching and motif repositioning, constrained rotation of helices around loop rings, and visualization of a user defined hybridization region between two strands. Drawings are exported as editable SVG or high-resolution PNG. The application is implemented as a single dependency-free HTML file that runs entirely in the browser and stores working state locally. This design makes the tool easy to distribute and suitable for rapid preparation of figures for manuscripts, presentations, and exploratory communication. AptaRender complements prediction and template-based visualization software by concentrating on lightweight, local, art directed figure construction. Across eight test cases, AptaRender reliably generated accurate, information-rich 2D nucleic acid structures and exported them in PNG and SVG formats, although specialized annotations and additional symbols required external editing.

title: Embedding kernels for sequence-function relationships.
abstract: A central challenge in biology is understanding how variation in biological sequences (DNA, RNA, and protein) impacts function. Recent advances in high-throughput techniques have enabled the measurement of such sequence-function relationships on an unprecedented scale. However, analyzing these complex datasets requires models that are both flexible and mathematically tractable. We consider Gaussian process regression, a Bayesian method that specifies a Gaussian prior distribution over sequence-function relationships. The prior is defined by a kernel function that encodes the expected covariance between pairs of sequences. We study a family of embedding kernels in which the covariance depends on the distance between sequences in a learned embedding space, making these kernels both expressive and interpretable. We show that linear embedding kernels generalize previously studied classes of kernels and can more flexibly express variability in the expected similarity between mutational effects across genetic backgrounds, allowing the resulting priors to encode more complex biological mechanisms such as RNA base-pairing. We implement these methods using a GPU-accelerated Gaussian process framework, allowing us to learn linear embeddings and make predictions with datasets containing hundreds of thousands of measurements. We find that our embedding kernels match or improve the predictive performance of other kernels across various high-throughput sequence-function datasets, including protein datasets ranging from short motifs to full-length proteins. Furthermore, the learned embedding spaces provide insight into biological mechanisms underlying sequence-function relationships.

title: Whole-plant visualization of endogenous RNA with an RNA-sensing fluorescence reporter toward single-molecule imaging.
abstract: Spatiotemporal mapping of endogenous RNA expression and trafficking in living plants remains challenging. Here, we introduce the plant endogenous RNA reporting system (PERS), an RNA-sensing fluorescent platform for in vivo visualization of unmodified native transcripts. PERS integrates an engineered target-binding allosteric RNA switch that sterically shields a miniature degron on a modular green fluorescent protein reporter, coupled with a SunTag-based signal amplification module. This design enables noninvasive, single molecule-sensitive imaging of plant endogenous RNAs with substantially improved signal-to-background performance, without detectable perturbation to plant growth or tested target-gene expression. Using PERS, we resolved subcellular localization and trafficking of individual RNAs and quantitatively tracked gene expression dynamics from single cells to whole plants across multiple contexts, including constitutive housekeeping genes, tissue-specific expression patterns, circadian rhythm oscillations, and acute stress-responsive programs. By enabling programmable, high-specificity detection of endogenous RNAs across scales, PERS provides a platform to map RNA localization and trafficking in vivo, opening avenues to dissect and engineer systemic signaling networks in plant biology.

title: EV-A71 3D enhances mitogen-activated protein kinases signaling cascades dependent on Y258 and I448.
abstract: Enterovirus A71 (EV-A71) infection activates host Mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK) signaling cascades, but the upstream viral factor triggering this activation remains unclear [1-3]. Here, by screening EV-A71 nonstructural proteins, we identified 3D as the only viral protein that markedly activated an activator protein-1 (AP-1) reporter. Mechanistically, 3D overexpression promoted extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1/2 (ERK1/2) and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) phosphorylation and enhanced c-Jun expression and phosphorylation. The 3D-Y258S and 3D-I448D mutants exhibited a shift from diffuse to punctate localization and lost this activation. Moreover, brefeldin A (BFA) treatment did not block 3D-induced AP-1 activation, indicating independence of BFA-sensitive ADP-ribosylation factor (Arfs) activation. Collectively, EV-A71 3D activates ERK-c-Jun-AP-1 axes in a Y258- and I448-dependent manner, independently of its RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) activity and Arfs activation, providing new insights into the non-replicase function of 3D and EV-A71 pathogenesis.

title: Microglial remodeling associated with protein-folding stress in progressive supranuclear palsy.
abstract: Microglia play a pivotal role in neurodegeneration, yet their responses to tau pathology remain incompletely understood. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing of amyloid-β plaque-free frontal lobe tissue from eight progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) cases and five controls and complemented this analysis with neuropathological and morphometric assessments in eight PSP and eight control cases. Microglia were resolved into five subclusters, among which protein-folding and endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-stress-related signatures were most prominent in the homeostatic microglial and border-associated macrophage-like subclusters in PSP. In neuropathological specimens, immunoreactive area fractions for BiP, a protein-folding chaperone, were significantly increased in PSP frontal gray and white matter. IBA1/BiP double-positive tissue area fractions were also significantly increased in white matter. MHC class II antigen-processing and presentation pathways were enriched in the homeostatic microglial subcluster. HLA-DR/DP/DQ-immunoreactive area fractions were increased in frontal gray and white matter and positively correlated with AT8-immunoreactive area fractions across PSP and control cases. Double immunofluorescence demonstrated a higher proportion of HLA-DR/DP/DQ-positive cells among IBA1-positive microglia in both compartments. Morphometric analysis showed increased process length and branching of IBA1-positive microglia, while P2Y12-immunoreactive area fractions were increased in frontal white matter, supporting the retention of a homeostatic marker. Additional analyses of the midbrain periaqueductal gray showed increased IBA1/BiP double-positive, HLA-DR-positive, and P2Y12-positive area fractions in PSP. In vitro, pharmacological induction of protein-folding stress in human microglial clone 3 (HMC3) cells partially reproduced selected features of this remodeling, including homeostatic gene upregulation and a transition toward process-bearing morphologies. Together, these findings identify a distinct microglial remodeling program in PSP characterized by preserved homeostatic features, protein-folding/ER-stress-related responses, enhanced MHC class II immunoreactivity, and increased ramification. This remodeling differs from the classical disease-associated microglia profile described in amyloid-driven neurodegeneration and supports the concept that microglial states are shaped by the molecular context of the underlying proteinopathy.

title: Molecular characterization of a novel amalgavirus infecting Atractylodes macrocephala in Zhejiang Province, China.
abstract: A novel double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) virus, tentatively named Atractylodes macrocephala amalgavirus 1 (AmAV1), was identified by high-throughput sequencing (HTS) of RNAs extracted from Atractylodes macrocephala plants exhibiting mosaic symptoms in Zhejiang Province, China. The complete genome of AmAV1 is 3,339 nucleotides (nt) in length and encodes two putative proteins: a coat protein (CP) from open reading frame 1 (ORF1) and an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) from the fused ORFs 1 and 2 expressed via a '+1' programmed ribosomal frameshifting (PRF) mechanism. The RdRp of AmAV1 shares the highest amino acid sequence identity of 61.1% with its homolog in Guizotia abyssinica amalgavirus 1 (accession no. DAZ91009.1). Phylogenetic analysis indicated that AmAV1 clusters within a clade of other amalgaviruses, supporting its classification in the genus Amalgavirus, family Amalgaviridae. This is the first report of a novel amalgavirus infecting A. macrocephala.

title: Universal Hyb-Seq Kits Perform Well Below the Species Level and Allow Cost-Effective Upscaling in Herbarium Genomics.
abstract: Target capture sequencing has enhanced the study of plant evolution and molecular ecology, particularly through the access to degraded DNA from herbarium specimens. Universal 'off-the-shelf' kits, such as Angiosperms-353, are cheap and readily available but are considered to insufficiently expose variation below the species level, because they are designed to target highly conserved regions. Here we present the first direct comparison between universal and customised target capture approaches below the species level. We test this in a group of near-identical genotypes from both herbarium and fresh material of the common dandelion (apomictic lineages in Taraxacum officinale F.H.Wigg.). An RNA-bait panel was designed to capture (i) highly variable loci normally obtained with a Genotyping-by-Sequencing (GBS) approach customised for dandelions; (ii) custom selected genes with potential for environmental adaptation, likely to harbour intraspecific genetic variation; (iii) conserved exons from universal kits (Angiosperms-353; Compositae-COS). Although exons from universal kits yield considerably less intraspecific genetic variation than both customised approaches, they still provided sufficient genetic variation to discriminate between near-identical genotypes of the same apomictic lineage. This demonstrates that universal kits can be used to discriminate highly similar genotypes, with positive implications for herbarium genomics studies on all groups of flowering plants. Given that universal kits save up to 5 months of full-time work (baits design), reduce the per-sample cost by up to 65% and remove the need for genomic reference data, this approach is recommended to increase the number of samples under budgetary constraints while still capturing considerable levels of intraspecific genetic variation.

title: [Retracted] Baicalin alleviates diabetes‑associated cognitive deficits via modulation of mitogen‑activated protein kinase signaling, brain‑derived neurotrophic factor and apoptosis.
abstract: Subsequently to the publication of the above article, a concerned reader drew to the Editor's attention that an inappropriate antibody was reported to have been used to probe for phosphorylated ERK (or p‑ERK): The catalogue number for the antibody was reported in the Materials and methods section to have been sc‑377400 (purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Inc.), whereas this antibody does not target p‑ERK, but protein kinase RNA‑like ER kinase (also known as EIF2AK3), having the acronym 'PERK'. In addition, it was noted that certain of the western blot data featured in Fig. 3 on p. 6381 appeared to be discontinuous, suggesting that certain of the blots had been included in the gels non‑contiguously. In view of the apparent anomalies that have been identified with the western blot data in Fig. 3, the Editor of Molecular Medicine Reports has decided that this paper should be retracted from the Journal on account of a lack of confidence in the presented data. The authors were asked for an explanation to account for these concerns, but the Editorial Office did not receive a reply. The Editor apologizes to the readership for any inconvenience caused. [Molecular Medicine Reports 12: 6377‑6383, 2015; DOI: 10.3892/mmr.2015.4219].

title: Exosomal proteins in prostate cancer progression: from mechanisms to diagnostic and therapeutic applications.
abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) remains a leading cause of cancer death in men, and the limitations of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing continue to delay diagnosis and confound risk stratification. Exosomes, small extracellular vesicles that can be recovered non-invasively from blood and urine, provide a window onto tumour biology, and the proteins they carry are the most readily measurable of their cargoes for clinical assay development. This review summarises how exosomal proteins sustain four programmes that jointly drive PCa progression: Wnt/β-catenin-dependent metastasis, angiogenesis, immune evasion and the suppression of ferroptosis, the iron-dependent, lipid-peroxidation-driven cell death to which treatment-resistant PCa is vulnerable. Each protein is considered together with its cell of origin, carcinoma cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts or tumour-associated macrophages, because the same molecule can act differently depending on the cell that released it. Key examples include GIPC2, which engages the Wnt co-receptor Fzd7 to activate β-catenin signalling; PGAM1, which binds γ-actin in endothelial cells to promote angiogenesis; exosomal PD-1 and PD-L1, which respectively activate myeloid-derived suppressor cells and suppress CD8+ T cells; and FTH1P8 together with CAF-derived miR-432-5p, which blunt ferroptosis and sustain docetaxel and antiandrogen resistance. The review also covers the diagnostic value of urinary exosomal proteins such as PSMA and PSA, the difference between these protein markers and the RNA-based ExoDx EPI test, and the emerging advances, from GMP-compliant manufacturing and single-vesicle quantification to regulatory guidance, that are beginning to overcome the barriers of isolation heterogeneity, scalability, immunogenicity and regulation.

title: Controlling CRISPR: a review of current anti-CRISPR technologies.
abstract: Anti-CRISPR systems are emerging as essential regulators of CRISPR-Cas technologies, providing a controllable "off-switch" for genome editing, transcriptional regulation, and gene-drive applications. This review surveys the expanding landscape of anti-CRISPR strategies, including naturally occurring Acr proteins, engineered Acr switches, small-molecule inhibitors, and nucleic acid-based inhibitors. Acr proteins, discovered in phages and other mobile genetic elements, exploit diverse mechanisms such as blocking CRISPR-Cas complex assembly, preventing target DNA or RNA binding, or directly inhibiting catalysis. Recent work has revealed additional noncanonical mechanisms, including RNA mimicry, host-factor hijacking, and enzymatic modifications of Cas proteins. In parallel, computational screening and machine-learning methods have accelerated discovery of Acr families and enabled de novo design of Cas13 inhibitors. This review also examines engineered control systems that make Acr activity conditional on chemical, light, miRNA, protease, or other environmental cues, enabling spatial and temporal regulation of CRISPR function. Small-molecule inhibitors and nucleic-acid inhibitors offer complementary CRISPR control, including the potential for improved delivery, tunable dosing, and modular design, though further assessment in therapeutic applications is necessary. Across applications, anti-CRISPRs have shown utility in improving editing precision, reducing toxicity, constraining gene drives, controlling CRISPRi/CRISPRa systems, and enhancing safety in therapeutic and agricultural contexts. Despite substantial progress, important challenges remain, including delivery, specificity across natural and engineered CRISPR variants, and governance. Future efforts will likely focus on rational design, multiplexed inhibition, and integration of anti-CRISPR systems into existing CRISPR-Cas therapeutic and environmental frameworks. As CRISPR continues to expand beyond the laboratory into medicine, agriculture, and ecological engineering, anti-CRISPR technologies will play a central role in enabling safer and more precise genome engineering.

title: Targeting STAU1 ameliorates disease phenotypes in TDP-43 ALS mice.
abstract: Altered RNA metabolism and impaired proteostasis are central to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). STAU1 is a multifunctional RNA-binding protein that regulates mRNA decay and trafficking, interacts with ATXN2, and is overabundant in neurodegenerative disease models. STAU1 overabundance activates mTOR signaling, impairs autophagy and stress-granule turnover, and thereby participates in a feed-forward circuit that further elevates STAU1 abundance. Here, we tested whether genetic and antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-mediated STAU1 lowering can interrupt this circuit in TDP-43-associated disease. Stau1 haploinsufficiency in Prp -TDP-43 Q331K mice improved motor performance and open-field measures, reduced TDP-43 and gliosis, normalized neuronal, apoptotic, and autophagy markers, restored TDP-43-dependent splicing, and attenuated transcriptomic abnormalities. Screening 2'- O -methoxyethyl (MOE) gapmer ASOs identified ASO-45, which lowered STAU1 in patient-derived fibroblasts and mouse CNS. Intracerebroventricular ASO-45 improved spinal-cord and motor-cortex phenotypes, restored splicing, and attenuated cortical transcriptomic abnormalities. In independent Thy1 -TDP-43 models, ASO-45 improved molecular markers and extended survival by 9.5-15.7%. These findings show that STAU1 lowering can disrupt a self-amplifying mTOR-autophagy-stress-granule axis and nominate STAU1-directed ASOs as a disease-modifying strategy for ALS/FTD.

title: STL1267 alters HIF-1α and REV-ERBα localization and transcriptional responses in CoCl 2 -treated HeLa cells.
abstract: REV-ERB nuclear receptors regulate gene expression and cellular metabolism, but their role in the response to hypoxia-associated stress remains unclear. We examined how the REV-ERB agonist STL1267 affects protein distribution and gene expression in HeLa cells exposed to cobalt chloride (CoCl 2 ). Immunofluorescence microscopy and RNA sequencing were used to compare vehicle-treated controls, cells exposed to CoCl 2 plus vehicle, and cells exposed to CoCl 2 plus STL1267. Representative images showed stronger nuclear HIF-1α staining after CoCl 2 exposure. Nuclear staining was less pronounced with STL1267, while REV-ERBα showed more extranuclear staining. CoCl 2 exposure altered 267 genes, and STL1267 treatment during CoCl 2 exposure altered 132 genes at a false discovery rate below 0.05. STL1267 increased ATF4 expression alongside genes involved in amino-acid synthesis and one-carbon metabolism, including ASNS, PHGDH, PSAT1, PSPH and MTHFD2. CTH and CHAC1 also increased, highlighting changes in sulfur-amino-acid metabolism and glutathione turnover. Among the genes induced by CoCl 2 , CA9, BNIP3 and LDHA decreased with STL1267, whereas HK2, PDK1 and VEGFA did not change significantly. STL1267 selectively reshapes hypoxia-associated gene expression and induces an ATF4-associated metabolic transcriptional program in CoCl 2 -treated HeLa cells, alongside qualitative changes in HIF-1α and REV-ERBα distribution. These findings identify a potential connection between protein compartmentalization and metabolic stress responses, providing a basis for investigating how REV-ERB ligands influence cellular adaptation to oxygen limitation.

title: A Molecular Glue that Regulates Processing of Non-Coding RNAs in Human Cells.
abstract: Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) are a major class of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) and essential components of the spliceosome. Chemical tools for perturbing snRNA structure and function are lacking, and ncRNAs have more generally been considered undruggable. Here we use chemical proteomics and cryo-electron microscopy to identify a covalent molecular glue HL-1B that stabilizes binding of the 3'-exonuclease TOE1 to the spliceosome in a catalytically competent state. We show that HL-1B triggers excess 3'-processing of snRNAs in human cells that is tunable by the expression levels of TOE1 and auxiliary splicing regulators like SNRPB2, which, in turn, create synthetic lethality interactions with HL-1B that correlate with the preferential modulation of intermediate exon inclusion splicing events. Our findings reveal a fundamental role for snRNA tail length in regulating spliceosome function and, more generally, a way to target ncRNAs with non-orthosteric small molecules that remodel the interactomes of RNA processing enzymes in cells.

title: Optogenetic RNA relocalization reveals causal neural function in vivo.
abstract: RNA localization dictates where translation occurs, yet its disease role is unclear because most assays manipulate abundance, not position. We develop an optogenetic CRISPR-dCas13 system (Opto-CRISPR-TO) that repositions endogenous RNAs with subcellular precision, second-scale kinetics, and reversibility, enabling causal tests in vivo . In cells, Opto-CRISPR-TO routes diverse RNAs to organelles and ribonucleoprotein granules with multiplex, bidirectional control, revealing distinct RNA behaviors in centrosomes and P-bodies. In mouse retina, acute (4-hour) mislocalization of Actb mRNA redirects β-actin protein, remodels synaptic architecture and cell positioning, and persistently impairs vision. Thus, RNA location governs proteome topology and neural circuit output, and brief mislocalization drives lasting dysfunction. The approach generalizes across targets, compartments, and cell types, establishing a framework for probing RNA localization mechanisms in development, plasticity, and degeneration.

title: Defining host factors required for dengue virus NS1-induced endothelial hyperpermeability and endothelial glycocalyx layer disruption.
abstract: Dengue virus (DENV) is a mosquito-borne positive-sense RNA virus belonging to the Flaviviridae family that poses a significant threat to global health. Clinical manifestations of DENV infection range from febrile to severe disease characterized by vascular leakage. The secreted DENV nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) contributes to endothelial dysfunction through interactions with endothelial cells, leading to disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx and intercellular junction complexes (IJC). However, host factors required for NS1-triggered endothelial dysfunction are not well understood. It is also unclear if NS1 highjacks different host factors and signaling pathways for glycocalyx and IJC disruption. To address these questions, we used a targeted genetic approach to identify host factors required either for NS1-triggered endothelial glycocalyx layer (EGL) disruption, as assessed by immunofluorescence assays, or for IJC disruption, as measured by transendothelial electrical resistance. After demonstrating the decoupled nature of EGL and IJC disruption in our models, we genetically depleted host factors with known roles in regulating endothelial barrier function and/or involvement in NS1 pathogenesis, including heparanase, cathepsin L, sialidases, and the PI3K/AKT/mTOR and β-catenin signaling pathways. Our results reveal a complex genetic landscape where NS1-induced disruption of EGL and IJCs involves both unique and shared host factors. Further, our data identify a direct role for β-catenin in NS1-induced endothelial dysfunction in vitro and in vivo . Overall, this work advances understanding of host factors required for DENV NS1-triggered endothelial dysfunction, revealing distinct intracellular pathways that are highjacked by NS1 to modulate barrier function, thus providing new insights into dengue-associated vascular leak. Dengue virus (DENV) is the most widespread arbovirus in the world, and its severe forms are characterized by endothelial dysfunction and vascular leakage. The DENV non-structural protein 1 (NS1) plays a significant role in disrupting the endothelial glycocalyx (EGL) and mislocalizing intercellular junction complexes (IJCs), two processes essential for endothelial dysfunction. However, the host factors involved in NS1-induced endothelial dysfunction, as well as the overlap between EGL and IJC dysfunction, remain unclear. To address this gap, we genetically disrupted various host factors involved in pathways modulating endothelial barrier function. Our data revealed a complex genetic landscape in which EGL and IJC are mechanistically decoupled and in which NS1-induced disruption of these barriers involves both specific and shared host factors. This work presents a new research framework enabling a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying NS1-induced pathogenesis and, consequently, the identification of new therapeutic approaches for severe forms of dengue.

title: Conserved Roles of Murine SAMHD1 Isoforms in Replication Fork Dynamics and Nascent DNA Processing.
abstract: Sterile alpha motif and histidine-aspartic acid domain-containing protein 1 (SAMHD1) is a deoxynucleoside triphosphate triphosphohydrolase (dNTPase) involved in intracellular nucleotide homeostasis, antiviral restriction, and genome maintenance. While human SAMHD1 (hSAMHD1) contributes to DNA replication fork stability and DNA double-strand break repair, the corresponding functions of murine SAMHD1 (mSAMHD1) remain poorly characterized. Here, we generated SAMHD1-deficient murine GL261 glioma cells using CRISPR/Cas9 to investigate mSAMHD1 function in DNA replication. SAMHD1 knockout increased intracellular dATP levels, altered replication fork dynamics, and reduced camptothecin (CPT)-induced nascent DNA degradation, supporting conserved replication-associated functions. RNA sequencing detected transcripts corresponding to all three annotated mSamhd1 isoforms, with isoform 1 predominating, followed by isoforms 2 and 3. To assess isoform-specific functions, individual murine isoforms were expressed in SAMHD1 -deficient human HEK293T cells, enabling direct comparison in a SAMHD1 -null background. Both major murine isoforms, mSAMHD1 isoforms 1 and 2, localized to the nucleus, exhibited nucleotide-dependent oligomerization and retained dNTPase activity. Notably, both isoforms restored replication fork dynamics and camptothecin (CPT)-induced nascent DNA degradation to levels largely comparable to hSAMHD1. In contrast, isoform 3 exhibited markedly reduced ectopic expression, consistent with its low endogenous transcript abundance in primary murine cells, limiting functional characterization. Together, these findings demonstrate that the two major murine SAMHD1 isoforms retain replication-associated functions of hSAMHD1 despite differences in their C-terminal regions. Furthermore, the established SAMHD1-deficient GL261 cells provide a model for future studies of SAMHD1 function in glioma and its tumor immune microenvironment. Although SAMHD1 has been extensively studied in human cells, its functions in murine DNA replication and replication fork maintenance remain incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that SAMHD1 deficiency impairs replication fork dynamics and reduces stress-induced nascent DNA degradation in murine glioma cells. We further characterize the expression of three annotated murine SAMHD1 isoforms and show that the two major isoforms can restore replication-associated functions in SAMHD1-deficient human cells. These findings support the functional conservation of SAMHD1 between humans and mice and establish a murine cellular model for investigating its contribution to genome maintenance. The generated GL261 SAMHD1-knockout cells provide a foundation for future studies of SAMHD1 in immunocompetent glioma models, where its effects on tumor biology and immune regulation can be investigated.

title: Disease Mutation-Guided Discovery of Peptide Inhibitors of the Dyskerin Dimer In H/ACA Ribonucleoproteins.
abstract: Hinge and ACA (H/ACA) ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) play key regulatory roles in ribosome biogenesis, splicing, and telomerase maintenance, and their activities are enhanced in cancer cells. The central component of H/ACA RNPs is the enzyme dyskerin (DKC1). DKC1 has high expression in multiple tumour types, and contributes to cancer hallmarks, tumour growth, and cellular immortalisation. DKC1 mutations also cause dyskeratosis congenita, a premature-ageing syndrome characterised by hindered ribosome biogenesis and shortened telomeres. We leveraged genetic information to devise a strategy to generate dyskerin inhibitors. Mapping of DKC1 mutations on the cryogenic electron microscopy structures of H/ACA RNP showed they alter the dyskerin/dyskerin protein-protein interaction in this complex. Based on this, we designed and synthesised peptides that inhibit dyskerin dimerisation and developed in vitro protein assays demonstrating protein engagement and interaction inhibition. Lead peptides reduced cell viability, protein synthesis, and cancer-related small nucleolar RNA levels in brain tumour cells (medulloblastoma and glioblastoma). Overexpression of DKC1 partially counteracted the effects of peptide inhibitors, consistent with modulation of dyskerin-dependent cellular processes. These results provide proof-of-concept that disruption of the dyskerin/dyskerin interaction can modulate H/ACA RNP function and support exploration of this interface as a potential therapeutic target.

title: Epigenome Editing in Endodontics: Current Evidence and Translational Prospects.
abstract: Epigenome editing permits locus-specific control of gene expression without intentionally changing the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence. This critical narrative perspective assesses the small direct dental evidence base, separates molecular target engagement from tissue repair and identifies experiments needed to judge therapeutic value. A focused narrative search examined PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception through September 17, 2026. Evidence was organised into five categories according to proximity to endodontic application. A reproducible PubMed verification search during revision identified 73 records and two unique studies eligible for the direct editing and programmable activation categories. Direct evidence is limited to locus-specific editing in human dental pulp stem cells. The FK506-binding protein 5 (FKBP5) study demonstrated promoter acetylation in cultured cells (n = 3 for chromatin immunoprecipitation), without editor-mediated repair in vivo. The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) study reported greater dentine mineral density after transplantation of activated cells (n = 5 in the microcomputed tomography analysis; p < 0.05), although its controls could not isolate the contribution of gene activation. Broader dental studies support regulatory roles for DNA methylation, histone modification and RNA methylation. Studies outside dentistry demonstrate durable and, in selected systems, reversible epigenetic silencing in vivo. Major unresolved issues are direct pulp delivery, cell specificity, duration, off-target effects, biodistribution and long-term safety. Epigenome editing could provide targeted control of reparative, regenerative and inflammatory responses in endodontics without intentional DNA sequence modification. Potential reversibility must be demonstrated for each target and editor. Current evidence supports mechanistic investigation; clinical development requires editor-attributable tissue benefit and an advantage over simpler interventions.

title: Virome analysis reveals an arthropod-specific RNA virus that enhances host adaptation to stress.
abstract: Viruses are obligate parasites that rely on host cellular machinery for replication and transmission. Accordingly, arthropod-associated viruses can establish neutral, beneficial, or pathogenic relationships. However, over the past two decades, metatranscriptome studies have uncovered diverse viromes that include many asymptomatic RNA viruses. Here we focus on newly discovered arthropod-specific RNA viruses whose biological functions and ecological significance remain largely unknown. We analyzed the virome of the two-spotted mite Tetranychus urticae, a globally distributed agricultural pest that infests more than 1100 plants. Among 153 transcriptome datasets, we identified five novel putative viral sequences. Together with all previously reported viruses in T. urticae, we took the 22 viruses as the whole virome and analyzed their dynamics across all 515 transcriptome datasets in NCBI, finding an average of five viruses per dataset. The most prevalent were Tetranychus urticae Nege/Kita-like virus (TuNKV) and Tetranychus urticae dicistro-like virus 1 (TuDV-1). These viruses also triggered robust RNAi responses in four field-collected mite populations, implying they are infectious. Intriguingly, TuNKV was asymptomatic but significantly enhanced host adaptation to abiotic and biotic stresses. We found that TuNKV structural protein 24 (SP24) interacted with host cuticle proteins (CPRs), and that silencing the CPRs also reduced viral titers and diminished the protection induced by TuNKV. Importantly, TuNKV enhanced host population growth during an ecological bottleneck caused by combined stress challenges. Our study demonstrates that viral reads account for a significant fraction of the T. urticae transcriptome and represent prevalent viruses with ecological relevance. In particular, TuNKV appears to enhance host survival during exposure to diverse environmental stresses. Moving beyond the conventional view of viruses solely as a burden to their hosts, these findings expand our knowledge of arthropod viruses and host-virus relationships. Video Abstract.

title: Decreased mechanosensitivity and metabolic reprogramming impair bone regeneration in type II diabetes: core mechanism and targeted scaffold design.
abstract: Bone regeneration in individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is significantly impaired, even when autologous bone grafts are used. However, previous studies have failed to elucidate the physiological mechanism, and effective treatments are lacking. This study investigated the underlying mechanisms and developed a targeted therapeutic strategy. We established a femoral condyle defect model in diabetic rats and performed autologous bone grafting. Multiomics sequencing analyses revealed core events that occurred in diabetic bone tissue. Seahorse XF analysis was used to detect cellular metabolic reprogramming. Calcium ion flow cytometry and YAP nuclear localization experiments confirmed the changes in mechanosensitivity in BMSCs from diabetic rats. Targeted scaffolds to repair diabetic bone defects were developed through Si ion surface modification and structural design and validated in the diabetic rat bone defect model. Proteomic and targeted energy metabolomics analyses revealed an imbalance in osteogenic/adipogenic differentiation and glycolytic dysfunction. RNA sequencing of BMSCs from diabetic rats revealed that reduced mechanosensitivity may be the core mechanism responsible for the alterations in cell fate. Flow cytometry with a calcium ion probe and YAP nuclear localization experiments confirmed the decreased mechanosensitivity of BMSCs from diabetic rats. Si-CaP was developed to increase glycolysis and the TPMS microstructure was designed to promote YAP nuclear translocation, thereby redirecting BMSCs toward osteogenic differentiation. In vivo experiments in a diabetic rat femoral condyle defect model demonstrated that the structured Si-CaP TPMS scaffold effectively promoted bone regeneration. T2DM-associated bone defect healing impairment is caused by metabolic reprogramming and reduced mechanosensitivity in BMSCs. Targeted modulation of metabolism and mechanosensitivity is an effective treatment for bone defects in T2DM rats.

title: Cas12m nuclease activation governed by intact RuvC active site and bipartite ssDNA kink.
abstract: The type V-M CRISPR-Cas12m effectors have been characterized as transcriptional silencers that defend bacteria against invading mobile genetic elements through robust DNA binding rather than target DNA cleavage. Here, using Escherichia coli-based negative selection screening, we identified two active Cas12m effectors, UnCas12m3 and UnCas12m4a, which cleave the target DNA in a CRISPR RNA-dependent manner. Cryo-electron microscopy structures of nuclease-active UnCas12m4a and nuclease-inactive TfCas12m3 reveal that Cas12m nuclease activation requires not only an intact RuvC catalytic triad but also a distinctive, bipartite single-stranded DNA kink to cause physical tension around the scissile phosphate. Guided by this mechanistic insight, we rationally restored the nuclease activity of inactive TfCas12m3 and MmCas12m2 through structure-guided engineering. These findings redefine the functional landscape of Cas12m enzymes and establish a framework for developing compact and efficient Cas12m-based genome-editing tools by substituting the structural elements responsible for nuclease catalysis and PAM recognition as separate, exchangeable molecular cassettes.

title: Viral tRNA-like structure hijacks host ribosomes for poly(A)-independent translation.
abstract: Positive-sense RNA viruses often use 3' tRNA-like structures (TLSs) instead of poly(A) tails to capture the host translation machinery. While TLSs resemble canonical tRNAs and engage host factors, their ability to directly recruit ribosomes has remained unresolved. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy snapshots of the histidine-accepting TLS (TLSHis) from tobacco mosaic virus bound to the tobacco 60S subunit, the 80S ribosome, and the 80S-tRNAiMet initiation complex. Across these states, TLSHis is consistently anchored to the L1 stalk of 60S, even under cycloheximide treatment, yet remains dynamic on the 40S subunit. Structural analysis shows that TLSHis transitions from the E-site to an adjacent Z-site to accommodate initiator tRNA. Functional assays show that TLSHis preferentially associates with ribosomal subunits over polysomes and can substitute for a poly(A) tail to promote robust cap-dependent translation. These results provide structural and mechanistic evidence that the viral tRNA mimic exploits the tRNA-exit channel to stabilize initiation-competent ribosomes and drive poly(A)-independent translation.

title: [Impacts of sulfur limitation on carbon flux and proteome resource allocation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae].
abstract: Sulfur is an essential element for the assembly and homeostasis of iron-sulfur clusters in cells. To elucidate carbon flux and proteome resource reallocation strategies of Saccharomyces cerevisiae under sulfur limitation, this study systematically investigated sulfur-limited chemostat cultures by integrating multi-omics analysis with the Pirt energy model. Metabolic flux analysis revealed that under aerobic conditions, tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle flux was markedly constrained [<0.3 mmol/(g DCW·h)], triggering overflow metabolism and resulting in a specific ethanol production rate of 11.38 mmol/(g DCW·h). Under anaerobic conditions, cellular metabolism primarily relied on glycolysis, with a maximum specific glucose uptake rate of 13.34 mmol/(g DCW·h), approximately twice that under aerobic conditions. Energy balance analysis showed that the non-growth-associated maintenance energy (mATP) under aerobic conditions reached 5.25 mmolATP/(g DCW·h), approximately twice that under anaerobic conditions. Proteomic analysis further revealed coordinated regulation of resource allocation by oxygen availability and specific growth rate. Under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions, cells upregulated ribosome biogenesis and RNA transport pathways during rapid growth to support proliferation, while enhancing molecular chaperones and proteasome systems at low growth rates (μ=0.05 h-1) to alleviate protein-folding stress. In addition, trehalose biosynthesis and the accumulation of glutamate and other metabolic intermediates indicated redirection of intracellular carbon and nitrogen resources to maintain cellular homeostasis. Notably, aerobic cells preferentially upregulated proteins associated with the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, whereas anaerobic cells significantly enhanced the expression of enzymes involved in glycolysis and lipid biosynthesis. Sulfur limitation maintained high substrate uptake rates and carbon metabolic fluxes despite substantial growth inhibition under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions. However, energy utilization efficiency differed between the two conditions. The maximum theoretical ATP biomass yield under aerobic sulfur limitation (15.3 g DCW/mol ATP) was higher than that under anaerobic sulfur limitation (9.74 g DCW/mol ATP). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that sulfur limitation enables partial decoupling between growth rate and carbon metabolic flux in S. cerevisiae, establishing a metabolically reallocated state with engineering potential. This work provides quantitative experimental evidence and theoretical support for the development of non-growth-associated yeast cell factories and high-efficiency biomanufacturing processes.

title: [Advances in in vivo directed evolution systems for microorganisms].
abstract: Conventional microbial strain engineering predominantly relies on iterative cycles of in vitro mutagenesis and rational design, a paradigm often constrained by limited library throughput and the unpredictable nature of complex phenotypes. To overcome these bottlenecks, researchers have shifted focus to the intracellular environment, developing in vivo directed evolution technologies that generate genetic diversity and enable selection directly within the host, thereby drastically shortening evolutionary timescales and greatly increasing the number of accessible beneficial mutations. This review systematically summarizes representative technologies and advances in this field from the past decade, organized by their mutation introduction mechanisms. It covers strategies ranging from early recombination-mediated integration of oligonucleotides or error-prone PCR products (e.g., MAGE and TRMR) to continuous evolution systems based on error-prone DNA polymerases [e.g., phage-assisted continuous evolution (PACE) and OrthoRep]; from Ty1 retrotransposon-mediated mutagenesis to targeted deaminase-based tools (e.g., MutaT7 and base editors); and emerging platforms driven by error-prone RNA polymerases or the NHEJ repair pathway. These technologies each possess distinct characteristics in mutational spectrum, targeting precision, and host applicability, collectively exhibiting three major trends: the shift of mutagenesis from in vitro to autonomous in vivo processes, the transition of operational modes from serial manual cycles to automated continuous processes, and the expanding of host range toward industrially relevant microorganisms. Building on these trends, the synergistic advancement of mutagenesis tools and screening methods promises to overcome the bottleneck of generating diversity without the tools for screening, propelling in vivo directed evolution toward a universal technology platform applicable to a broad range of chassis organisms and complex phenotypes. This review systematically summarizes the principles, advantages, and limitations of various technologies, discusses future directions for the synergistic advancement of mutagenesis tools and screening methods, and provides guidance for researchers in selecting appropriate technologies based on specific evolutionary objectives, offering important insights for advancing in vivo directed evolution toward a universal technology platform.

title: Enterovirus 71 Infection Orchestrates One-Carbon Metabolism and S-Adenosylmethionine Generation to Drive Inflammation-Related Chromatin Methylation.
abstract: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is the major methyl donor for histone, DNA, and RNA methylation, thereby linking cellular metabolism to chromatin state and gene transcription. However, how enterovirus 71 (EV71) infection regulates SAM generation and how SAM-dependent methylation contributes to host gene regulation remain unclear. Here, we show that EV71 infection enhances glucose-, serine-, and methionine-derived metabolic inputs into the methionine cycle and promotes SAM generation through de novo ATP synthesis. Mechanistically, EV71 2Apro cleaves ubiquitin-protein ligase E3 component n-recognin 4 (UBR4), thereby reducing UBR4-mediated MAT2A ubiquitination and stabilizing MAT2A to support SAM production. We further show that EV71 3Cpro promotes SETD2-dependent trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 36 (H3K36me3), which is associated with DNMT3B enrichment and gene-body DNA methylation at inflammatory and cell-death-associated genes. In parallel, EV71 3Dpol interacts with METTL14, a core component of the m6A methyltransferase complex, and contributes to m6A deposition on host transcripts. Disrupting the 2Apro/UBR4, 3Cpro/SETD2, 3Cpro/DNMT3B, or 3Dpol/METTL14 interactions using designed cell-penetrating peptides reduced EV71-induced methylation changes, viral replication, inflammatory responses, and tissue injury. Together, our findings reveal a metabolic-epigenetic regulatory axis by which EV71 rewires one-carbon metabolism and SAM availability to promote methylation-dependent host gene expression and inflammatory pathogenesis.

title: The transcription factor ATF3 promotes angiogenesis in adipose tissue eosinophils.
abstract: Adipose tissue-resident eosinophils contribute to adipose tissue homeostasis and metabolic regulation and have a distinct transcriptional profile compared with circulating eosinophils. However, the transcriptional regulators that contribute to their tissue-specific functions remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of activating transcription factor (ATF3), which was enriched in adipose tissue-resident eosinophils compared with blood eosinophils. Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated ATF3 deletion and RNA sequencing in the human eosinophilic leukemia cell line EoL-1, we found that ATF3 regulated a broad transcriptional program, including suppression of pro-inflammatory pathways and promotion of genes associated with angiogenesis. ATF3 deletion reduced VEGFA expression and secretion in EoL-1 cells, and chromatin immunoprecipitation demonstrated ATF3 binding at the VEGFA promoter, supporting direct regulation of VEGFA in this eosinophilic cell model. In mice, genetic elevation of eosinophil numbers increased adipose tissue VEGFA abundance and endothelial cell representation. Conversely, eosinophil-specific Atf3 deletion did not significantly alter Vegfa transcript abundance in primary adipose eosinophils but was associated with reduced VEGFA protein abundance and endothelial cell representation in visceral adipose tissue. Together, these findings identify ATF3 as a regulator of tissue-supportive and pro-angiogenic programs in eosinophils and support a role for eosinophil-intrinsic ATF3 in maintaining the vascular environment of visceral adipose tissue.

title: METTL3-Mediated m6A Methylation of Malat1 is Associated With Macrophage Polarization and Sepsis-Associated Acute Lung Injury.
abstract: The present investigation explores the association of methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3)-the catalytic component responsible for depositing N6-methyladenosine (m6A) marks-with the pathogenesis of acute lung injury (ALI) within septic contexts. We aim to investigate its relationship with Malat1 m6A modification, the Malat1/mmu-miR-129-5p/Pax6-Zeb2 competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) network, and macrophage polarization, along with the underlying molecular mechanisms in an experimental model. An endotoxin-induced ALI model, a classic experimental paradigm for sepsis-associated ALI, was generated in vivo by intraperitoneal injection of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) into specific pathogen-free C57BL/6 mice. Prior to model establishment, mice received intravenous injections of Mettl3-silencing lentivirus for intervention. The degree of lung injury, inflammatory cytokine levels, expression of core molecules, and Malat1 m6A methylation levels were assessed. In vitro, an inflammatory model was created by stimulating RAW264.7 macrophages with LPS. Molecular interactions and regulatory functions were examined. LPS-induced ALI model mice exhibited significant upregulation of Mettl3, Malat1, Pax6, and Zeb2 transcripts in lung tissue, alongside notable downregulation of mmu-miR-129-5p. Malat1 m6A methylation levels were also significantly increased. These changes were tightly linked to pro-inflammatory M1 phenotypic polarization of macrophages and lung tissue damage (all P < 0.001). Silencing Mettl3 significantly reduced Malat1 m6A methylation levels, reversed the aberrant expression of the downstream regulatory axis, inhibited pro-inflammatory macrophage activation, and alleviated local and systemic inflammation, pulmonary edema, and lung injury (all P < 0.001). Mechanistic studies indicated that Malat1 acts as a molecular sponge for mmu-miR-129-5p, a microRNA that directly interacts with the Pax6 3'UTR, thereby regulating PAX6 and ZEB2 protein expression in a ceRNA-dependent manner (all P < 0.001). Rescue experiments suggested that the Malat1/mmu-miR-129-5p axis, along with downstream PAX6-ZEB2 signaling, is involved in the regulatory effect of METTL3 on macrophage phenotypic differentiation and the associated inflammatory processes within the LPS-induced inflammatory model. METTL3 is aberrantly overexpressed in the LPS-induced model of sepsis-associated ALI. This elevation is closely associated with METTL3-dependent m6A methylation of Malat1, which in turn is associated with its subsequent upregulation. Mettl3-dependent m6A modification of Malat1 is associated with dysregulation of the Malat1/mmu-miR-129-5p/Pax6-Zeb2 ceRNA network and may contribute to the pathogenesis of sepsis-associated pulmonary injury, a mechanism closely linked to pro-inflammatory M1 macrophage polarization. These findings provide a novel potential epigenetic target and experimental basis for the prevention and treatment of sepsis-associated ALI.

title: ALKBH5 mediates m⁶A modification of BARD1 to regulate the proliferation and differentiation of chicken myoblasts.
abstract: Skeletal muscle development represents a key economic trait in broiler breeding, and N⁶-methyladenosine (m⁶A) modification plays a critical role in post-transcriptional gene regulation during myogenesis. AlkB homolog 5 (ALKBH5) is a major m⁶A demethylase, whereas BRCA1-associated RING domain protein 1 (BARD1) is implicated in cell cycle control. Here, we employed both overexpression and RNA interference approaches to systematically investigate the roles of ALKBH5 and BARD1 in the proliferation and differentiation of chicken primary myoblasts (CPMs). We found that ALKBH5 significantly suppressed myoblast proliferation and promoted differentiation. Mechanistically, ALKBH5 reduced both global m⁶A levels and the m⁶A abundance on BARD1 mRNA, thereby decreasing BARD1 mRNA stability and downregulating its expression. Functionally, BARD1 exerted opposing effects, enhancing myoblast proliferation and inhibiting differentiation. Notably, introducing synonymous mutations at the m⁶A modification sites of BARD1 substantially attenuated its pro-proliferative and anti-differentiation activities. Collectively, these findings reveal that ALKBH5 regulates the expression and function of BARD1 through m⁶A demethylation, thereby modulating the proliferation and differentiation of CPMs. This study provides novel mechanistic insights into the epitranscriptomic regulation of skeletal muscle development.

title: The nucleolar pathway leading to autoimmune diseases.
abstract: Autoantibodies targeting nucleolar components exhibit a correlation with autoimmune pathologies. Mechanisms causing anti-nucleolar antibodies appear to be contingent upon nucleolar activity under stress. Nucleoli facilitate numerous critical functions, such as RNA folding, nucleoprotein assembly (e.g. ribosomes), DNA repair, and maintenance of heterochromatin. Extensive stress requiring DNA repair and/or protein replenishment can cause significant nucleolar dynamics, potentially disrupting epigenetic control in peri-nucleolar chromatin. This complicated scenario warrants further study. For example, altered gene expression could be involved, such as from normally suppressed Alu elements and fully functional LINE1 reverse transcriptases in peri-nucleolar chromatin. An abundance of Alu RNA and/or reverse transcribed Alu DNA could compete for binding nucleolin, an important protein in nucleolar structure, disrupting nucleolar integrity and lead to an autoimmune reaction to abnormal molecular complexes. Here, we present a perspective discussing possible involvement of nucleoli in autoimmune diseases, detailing proposed scenarios for disease onset.

title: Essential transcriptional regulators of cement proteins during barnacle settlement.
abstract: Underwater bioadhesion, which is a vital property for the survival and reproduction of many aquatic benthic organisms, has inspired the design of biomimetic materials. However, there is little information on the transcriptional regulatory mechanisms governing the expression of bioadhesives. Barnacles are well known for their strong adhesion to marine substrates, which arises from their unique cement proteins (CPs). In this work, we identified 145 transcription factors (TFs) that were potentially associated with cyprid settlement in the barnacle Amphibalanus amphitrite using genome-wide TF screening combined with weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Specifically, we demonstrated that PRRX2 activated the expression of a barnacle CP, Aacp19k-like, by binding to an AATTA motif located between -185 and -181 bp of its promoter. The gene expression of another CP gene, Aacp100k, was positively regulated by two TFs, SGF3 and NKX6.2, which targeted distinct cis-elements of TATGAA at -560 to -555 bp and CTCATCAAC at +325 to +333 bp, respectively. In vivo localization and RNA interference assays further confirmed that PRRX2, SGF3, and NKX6.2 are essential for cyprid settlement, as evidenced by their co-localization with Aacp19k-like and Aacp100k in the cement glands and the significant decrease in settlement rates that occurs following knockdown of these genes. Phylogenetic analysis indicated the conservation of PRRX2, SGF3, and NKX6.2 within different barnacle species. Overall, the findings of this study reveal the key transcriptional regulators of barnacle CPs and provide new mechanistic insights into underwater adhesion.

title: Nuclear Receptor 4A1 (NR4A1) and NR4A2 Regulate Expression of O6-Methylguanine-DNA-Methyltransferase (MGMT) in Glioblastoma and Can Be Targeted by NR4A1/2 Ligands.
abstract: Purpose Glioblastoma (GBM) is highly malignant and aggressive with limited treatment options. Resistance to the standard of care temozolomide (TMZ) is associated with expression of O 6 -methylguanine-DNA-methyltransferase (MGMT). This study investigates whether orphan nuclear receptor 4A1 (NR4A1) and NR4A2 regulate MGMT expression in GBM cells and whether DIM-3,5 compounds decrease MGMT expression and could be used to enhance TMZ efficacy in GBM cells. Methods Human and mouse GBM cell lines were used. Cells were treated with DIM-3,5 compounds and TMZ to evaluate cell proliferation. RNA interference was used to knockdown NR4A1/2, Sp1, or MGMT. MGMT mRNA and protein expression was measured using qrt-PCR and Western blotting. Luciferase reporter assays examined MGMT promoter activity, while chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays investigated transcription factor interactions on the MGMT promoter. Results DIM-3,5 compounds significantly decreased GBM cell proliferation in all cell lines. DIM-3,5 compounds or knockdown of NR4A1/2 or Sp1 significantly decreased MGMT mRNA, protein, and luciferase promoter expression in all cell lines. ChIP analysis demonstrated that NR4A1 and NR4A2 regulate MGMT through interactions with a NBRE motif and Sp1 regulates MGMT through GC-rich promoter regions. Additionally, MGMT knockdown increased TMZ-induced cytotoxicity in GBM cells. Conclusion This study shows that NR4A1/2/Sp1 are involved in MGMT regulation through complex mechanisms that include regulation by Sp1 alone and by direct interaction of NR4A1 and NR4A2 as monomers with an NBRE motif. DIM-3,5 ligands act as inverse NR4A1/2 agonists and downregulate MGMT expression in GBM cells.

title: Learning spatial cellular state through 3D reconstruction of the cell.
abstract: Subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics localizes individual RNA transcripts within cells with high-precision. Existing methods for identifying spatially organized cell populations rely on cellular niches defined by neighboring cells, leaving open whether such populations can be identified from individual-cell representations alone. Moreover, representations that jointly capture transcript identity and three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization have not been systematically learned or biologically evaluated. Here we present a representation learning framework that models each cell as a gene-annotated point cloud of transcripts and trains a rotation-equivariant neural network to reconstruct 3D cell shape, yielding spatially informed transcript embeddings. We further aggregate these embeddings into a cell-state representation that summarizes transcript-level spatial patterns. Our framework outperforms existing point-cloud-based 3D reconstruction methods on cell-shape reconstruction. In MERFISH human uterine cancer, combining the learned embeddings with gene expression improved prediction of CD45RO protein intensity over both gene expression alone and niche-based embeddings. Applied to MERFISH human liver cancer and Xenium human lung datasets, our framework identified distinct spatial patterns between cell populations, including spatially organized subpopulations marked by disease-associated gene expression and patterns associated with pathological tissue structures. Together, these results show that learning transcript representations through 3D cell reconstruction provides a novel approach to capture cell-state heterogeneity and biologically relevant spatial organization in subcellular spatial transcriptomics.

title: A Cis-element in magu-2 mediates apical mRNA localization via active transport in C. elegans.
abstract: mRNA subcellular localization is a key mechanism of post-transcriptional gene regulation and is widely conserved across cell types and species. Although increasing evidence suggests that transcripts associated with epithelial polarity also undergo asymmetric subcellular distribution, the trafficking patterns and regulatory mechanisms governing this process remain elusive. MAGU-2, the Caenorhabditis elegans ortholog of the Drosophila polarity gene stardust (sdt), has previously been reported to demonstrate apical mRNA enrichment. In this study, a truncation screen of magu-2 exon 3 identified a 270-nt SH3 domain-containing fragment sufficient to direct apical localization of both its encoded mRNA and the truncated MAGU-2 protein. Live imaging, RNAi-mediated knockdown of DHC-1, BicD, or EGAL-1, and nocodazole treatment revealed that this mRNA undergoes active transport and that apical targeting is disrupted upon impairment of dynein/BicD/Egalitarian function or microtubule integrity, implicating the conserved dynein/BicD/Egalitarian axis in magu-2 mRNA trafficking. While deletion of this 270-nt element exerted no overt effect on epithelial polarity or development, these findings provide insight into the active transport of epithelial polarity-related transcripts and position magu-2 as a useful model for dissecting cis-elements and trans-acting factors modulating subcellular RNA localization.

title: Stress-Induced Astrocytic ABCA1 Deficiency Caused Cholesterol Accumulation to Promote Synaptic Dysregulation and Behavioral Abnormalities.
abstract: Astrocytes supply cholesterol to neurons to support synaptic function, but how chronic stress disrupts this metabolic interaction remains unclear. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing revealed reduced ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) expression in hippocampal astrocytes of mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS). Chronic stress was also associated with reduced astrocytic liver X receptor (LXR) protein, cholesterol accumulation, inflammatory astrocyte reactivity, impaired dorsal Cornu Ammonis 1 (CA1) synaptic transmission and neuronal excitability, and depression-like behaviors. Astrocyte-targeted ABCA1 overexpression ameliorated these metabolic, inflammatory, electrophysiological, and behavioral disorders. Conversely, astrocytic LXRα/β knockdown or pharmacological LXR inhibition reduced ABCA1 expression and reproduced key stress-associated phenotypes. Restoring ABCA1 expression substantially reversed the abnormalities induced by astrocytic LXRα/β knockdown, supporting ABCA1 as an important functional mediator of LXR-associated dysfunction. Pharmacological LXR activation and cyclodextrin-mediated cholesterol reduction produced complementary improvements. Together, these findings identify impaired cholesterol handling in in dorsal CA1 astrocytes as a mechanistic link connecting chronic stress, neuroinflammation, and neuronal dysfunction, suggest that restoring astrocytic cholesterol homeostasis may mitigate depression-related pathology.

title: Novel primer sets for detecting satsuma dwarf virus using conventional RT-PCR and SYBR Green RT-qPCR.
abstract: Satsuma dwarf virus (SDV) exhibits substantial genetic diversity, which may compromise diagnostic reliability through primer-template mismatches. We developed two degenerate primer sets for SDV detection by conventional one-step reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) and one-step SYBR Green quantitative RT-PCR (RT-qPCR). To expand the sequence dataset for primer design, we determined the complete genome sequence of ND-2, a Japanese isolate belonging to the Natsudaidai dwarf virus subgroup. Sixteen candidate primer sets were designed using full-length RNA1 and RNA2 sequences from 15 reference isolates. Following three-stage screening, SD-RNA2-det1, producing a 118-bp amplicon, was selected for RT-qPCR, whereas SD-RNA2-det3, producing a 368-bp amplicon, was selected for conventional RT-PCR and direct sequencing. Isolate-specific standard curves generated using purified in vitro-transcribed RNA showed high linearity across the defined quantitative ranges (R² = 0.993-0.999). Using serially diluted infected-plant total RNA, SD-RNA2-det1 produced target-specific amplification across nine representative isolates, although quantitative performance varied among isolates. Under standardized conventional RT-PCR conditions, SD-RNA2-det3 generally produced readily interpretable single-band patterns when evaluated against three previously reported primer sets. These complementary assays provide a basis for SDV detection, quantitative estimation of viral RNA, and preliminary strain-group assignment, although further validation with field samples and additional genetic variants is required.

title: Structural and functional analysis of the Chast-NUCB1 interaction in cardiac hypertrophy.
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are emerging regulators in cardiac diseases and their expression profiles are often altered during pathophysiological conditions. In our study, we focused on a cardiomyocyte-enriched lncRNA called cardiac hypertrophy-associated transcript (Chast), whose precise molecular mechanism underlying its action in cardiac pathology remains poorly understood. To understand the function of lncRNA Chast, we performed a proteomic analysis of the Chast interactome to identify potential binding partners contributing to its specific function, and found a bona fide protein partner, nucleobindin-1 (NUCB1), involved in calcium homeostasis. Systematic truncation mapping and biophysical studies revealed that NUCB1 binds a 73-nucleotide-long helical RNA domain (Chast H2) with sub-micromolar affinity. CD-spectroscopy studies demonstrate that NUCB1 binding induces structural rearrangements of the Chast H2 motif, consistent with its RNA-chaperone-like activity. We also show that both Ca2+-binding domain and leucine zipper domain of NUCB1 are required for optimal RNA interaction and structural remodeling. Functionally, hypertrophic stimulation of cardiomyocytes results in the production of a 27-kDa NUCB1 cleavage fragment, consistent with caspase-mediated cleavage. Overexpression of full-length Chast markedly increases NUCB1 cleavage and promotes hypertrophic growth, whereas Chast knockdown reduces the cleavage. Collectively, our findings uncover a previously unknown Chast-NUCB1 regulatory axis, reveal the structural basis of their interaction, and identify Chast as a protease-cofactor lncRNA that amplifies hypertrophic signaling.

title: Western and high-fat diets differentially shape the cutaneous transcriptome in imiquimod-induced psoriasiform dermatitis.
abstract: Obesity is among the most consistent comorbidities of psoriasis, yet whether different obesogenic diets aggravate psoriasiform inflammation through shared or distinct inflammatory response remains unclear. We compared a Western diet (WD) and a high-fat diet (HFD) in a murine imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasiform dermatitis model. Male C57BL/6 mice were fed a reference diet (RD), HFD, or WD for 12 weeks before topical IMQ, and disease severity was assessed clinically, histologically, and by qRT-PCR. To characterize diet-associated transcriptional differences, skin RNA sequencing was performed as a direct comparison between WD-IMQ and HFD-IMQ groups. Both WD- and HFD-IMQ increased PASI scores, epidermal thickness, and spleen index relative to RD-IMQ, with WD-IMQ skin showing the greatest epidermal hyperplasia. Although Il17a and Il23 expressions were comparable between the two obesogenic diets, transcriptomic profiling revealed distinct immune signatures. Relative to HFD, WD-IMQ skin was enriched for innate immune, complement, and acute-phase programs including genes encoding serum amyloid A proteins (Saa1, Saa2, Saa3), C3, Hp, and neutrophil-associated mediators. Conversely, HFD-IMQ skin was enriched for antigen presentation and T-cell-receptor signaling, including (Cd3d, Cd3e, Cd3g, Lat, Itk, Icos, Pdcd1). QRT-PCR validation across all three diet groups reproduced these reciprocal expression patterns. Protein-protein interaction analysis supported a divergence between the innate/acute-phase module in WD-IMQ and the adaptive/TCR-signaling module in HFD-IMQ, whereas immune cell deconvolution, being computational, was considered hypothesis-generating. These findings indicate that different obesogenic diets elicit distinct relative inflammatory and immune transcriptional signatures during psoriasiform skin inflammation and suggest that dietary composition, in addition to adiposity, may contribute to heterogeneity in obesity-associated psoriasis.

title: Xist deletion in T cells protects against influenza-induced lung injury.
abstract: Sex differences in antiviral immunity are well established, yet the contribution of X-Chromosome Inactivation (XCI) to T cell responses during infection is unknown. Here, we identify an unexpected role for Xist RNA in shaping T cell immunity and pulmonary injury following influenza infection. We show that the inactive X chromosome (Xi) in pulmonary CD4+ and CD8+ T cells undergoes dynamic epigenetic remodeling, with limited Xist RNA localization, differential enrichment of H3K27me3 and H2AK119Ub modifications, and activation-dependent XCI escape of immune-related genes, including Il2rg and Cxcr3 . Remarkably, T cell-specific Xist deletion protects female mice from influenza-induced weight loss and pulmonary pathology despite comparable early viral burdens. Transcriptomic profiling reveals increased expression of X-linked escape genes and antiviral and interferon-responsive genes, particularly in CD8+ T cells. Furthermore, Xist-deficient CD4 + and CD8 + antigen-experienced (CD44 + CD11a + ) T cells exhibit increased biallelic Cxcr3 expression, elevated pulmonary Cxcr3 protein levels, and enhanced IFN-γ and TNF responses following ex vivo stimulation. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for Xist RNA in regulating female antiviral T cell responses and demonstrate that enhanced T cell effector potential can accompany reduced infection-associated pulmonary injury.

title: Brain disorder mechanisms and therapeutic targets identified from developmental, cell-specific gene regulation.
abstract: Genetic variation influences brain physiology and disease across cell types and development. We integrated whole-genome sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and single-nucleus multiome profiling from 231 human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex donors spanning six postconceptional weeks to 92 years. Across 24 brain-related traits, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric genetic risk was enriched in neuronal transcriptomic and chromatin profiles, whereas neurodegenerative risk was enriched in microglia. Thousands of expression, chromatin accessibility, and splicing quantitative trait loci revealed developmental and cell-type-specific regulatory effects. Colocalization linked multiple sclerosis risk to AHI1 expression in prenatal neurons and problematic alcohol use to GPX1 expression in postnatal glia. Leveraging dynamic cis-regulatory elements, we identified therapeutic candidates for haploinsufficient neurodevelopmental disorders, including a SOX5 enhancer whose CRISPR activation increased transcript and protein abundance. Together, these findings establish a publicly accessible genomic resource for resolving the developmental and cellular contexts of genetic risk and identifying therapeutic targets in the human brain. Biology : Chromatin and expression analyses reveal cell-type and developmental dynamics of brain disorder genes and variants. Atlas : Cell-type-resolved QTLs reveal dynamic genetic regulation during brain development. Mechanisms : Prenatal neuronal eQTLs implicate AHI1 in multiple sclerosis mechanisms. Therapy : CRISPR activation of an enhancer increases SOX5 mRNA and protein expression. Resource : BrainVar website enables interactive exploration of genetic regulation during brain development.

title: Transcriptome-informed selection and validation of reference genes for RT-qPCR normalization in Cuphea hookeriana across tissues and under low-temperature stress.
abstract: Reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) is widely used to quantify gene expression, but reliable normalization requires reference genes with stable expression in the species, tissues, and experimental conditions being examined. Cuphea hookeriana is an ornamental shrub whose wider landscape application is limited by poor cold tolerance. However, no validated reference genes have been reported for RT-qPCR normalization in this species. In this study, twelve candidate reference genes were selected from a C. hookeriana leaf transcriptome generated during a 5 °C low-temperature time course and deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject accession number PRJNA1117973. The candidates comprised elongation factor 1-alpha (EF1α), DnaJ heat shock protein (DNAJ), cyclophilin (CYP), glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH), actin (ACT), 18 S ribosomal RNA (18 S rRNA), eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (EIF2), tubulin (TUB), protein phosphatase 2 A (PP2A), acyl carrier protein (ACP), ubiquitin (UBQ), and ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (UBC). Their expression stability was evaluated in roots, stems, leaves, and flowers and in leaves exposed to 5 °C for 0, 12, 24, 36, and 48 h. The amplification efficiencies ranged from 92.41% to 104.50%, with correlation coefficients of 0.992-0.999. geNorm pairwise-variation analysis indicated that three reference genes were required for the different-tissue dataset, whereas two were sufficient for the low-temperature-treatment and pooled datasets. Accordingly, the validation analysis used ACP, UBC, and EF1α for tissues and 18 S rRNA and EIF2 for low-temperature-treated samples. One-way ANOVA of ΔCq values showed significant differences among tissues for CSLD and among treatment times for MYB11. Normalization using the least stable single genes, TUB or UBQ, produced group-dependent relative-expression estimates that differed significantly from those obtained using the geNorm-recommended combinations. This study identifies condition-specific reference-gene combinations for RT-qPCR analysis in C. hookeriana. The geometric mean of ACP, UBC, and EF1α is recommended for comparisons among tissues; 18 S rRNA and EIF2 are recommended for samples collected during the 5 °C treatment; and EIF2 and ACT are recommended for the pooled dataset containing all tissue and low-temperature-treatment samples.

title: Ferrostatin-1 exerts anti-inflammatory effects on experimental autoimmune uveitis rats via ferroptosis inhibition.
abstract: Autoimmune uveitis (AU)f is a severe inflammatory disorder of the eye that can compromise vision, while available treatment options remain inadequate. Ferroptosis is a regulated cell death pathway driven by iron accumulation. It has arisen as a potential contributor to inflammatory and autoimmune conditions, although its involvement in experimental autoimmune uveitis (EAU) has yet to be fully elucidated. This study investigated the involvement of ferroptosis in EAU and evaluated the therapeutic potential of the ferroptosis inhibitor Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1). EAU was established in Lewis rats following immunization with IRBP R16 peptide. Rats were divided into control, EAU, and EAU+Fer-1 groups. Retinal RNA sequencing was performed, followed by GO and KEGG enrichment analyses. Disease severity was evaluated clinically and histopathologically. Western blotting was used to assess SLC7A11, GPX4, and TfR1, while MDA, ROS, and GSH levels were measured to examine oxidative stress. Mitochondrial ultrastructural changes were inspected using transmission electron microscopy. Transcriptomic analysis revealed significant enrichment of ferroptosis-associated pathways in EAU retinas. EAU was accompanied by reduced expression of SLC7A11 and GPX4, increased TfR1 expression, elevated ROS and MDA levels, decreased GSH content, and characteristic mitochondrial alterations consistent with ferroptosis. Fer-1 treatment significantly reduced clinical and histopathological manifestations of ocular inflammation, improved retinal structural integrity, restored ferroptosis-related protein expression, attenuated oxidative stress, and alleviated mitochondrial abnormalities. Ferroptosis is associated with retinal inflammation and tissue injury in EAU. Pharmacological inhibition of ferroptosis by Fer-1 mitigated ocular inflammation and retinal damage while reversing multiple ferroptosis-related molecular and biochemical alterations. These findings identify ferroptosis as a promising target for therapeutic intervention in autoimmune uveitis and provide a rationale for further investigation of ferroptosis-targeted strategies in ocular inflammatory diseases.

title: Silent Regulators, Loud Impact: The Role of Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in the Regulation of Parkinson's Disease and Related Genes.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by a spectrum of neurological and non-neurological symptoms. How, when, or why the disease starts is still largely unknown. The predominant pathology has been motor symptoms arising from the death of dopaminergic neurons with α-synuclein protein aggregation; however, several alternative hypotheses have emerged that lead to differential disease onset. Although age, genetic, and environmental factors have been shown to be the leading causes of PD, growing evidence suggests that the non-coding regions of the human genome contribute more to disease pathology than previously known. One particular type of non-coding element, long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), has emerged as an important regulator of PD pathogenesis by modulating key genes and disease-relevant pathways. Recent studies highlight the involvement of lncRNAs in regulating PD-associated genes, including LRRK2, SNCA, PINK1/PRKN, and in cellular processes such as neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, autophagy, and α-synuclein aggregation. Several lncRNAs, including HOTAIR, MALAT1, and NEAT1, are differentially expressed in PD models and patient tissues, where they influence neuronal survival and stress responses through mechanisms such as microRNA (miRNAs) sponging, chromatin modification, and paraspeckle formation.
